stem: What is 'effective atomic number' (\(\text{EAN}\))? Calculate the effective atomic number of the central metal atom in the following compounds: \(\ \ \ \ \ \ \ a.\text{K}_{4}\left\lbrack \text{Fe}\left( \text{CN} \right)_{6} \right\rbrack\ \ \ \ \ \text{Fe (Z=26)}\) \(\ \ \ \ \ \ \text{b}\). \(\text{Cr}\left( \text{CO} \right)_{6}\) Cr(\(\text{Z} = 24\)).
solution:
**Effective atomic number (EAN)** is the total number of electrons on the central metal atom or ion of a complex AFTER it has accepted the electron pairs donated by the ligands. It is counted as

\(\mathrm{EAN} =\) (atomic number of the metal) \(-\) (oxidation state of the metal) \(+\ 2 \times\) (number of coordinate bonds formed by the ligands)

Sidgwick noticed that in many stable complexes this number comes out equal to the atomic number of the nearest noble gas.

**a. \(\mathrm{K_4[Fe(CN)_6]}\)**

The four potassium ions carry \(+4\) between them, so the coordination sphere is \(\mathrm{[Fe(CN)_6]^{4\ominus}}\). Each cyanide is \(-1\):

\(x + 6(-1) = -4\), so \(x = +2\), i.e. \(\mathrm{Fe^{2\oplus}}\).

Six monodentate cyanide ligands donate six electron pairs, so the coordination number is 6.

\(\mathrm{EAN} = 26 - 2 + 2(6) = 26 - 2 + 12\)

\(\therefore\ \mathrm{EAN} = 36\)

**b. \(\mathrm{Cr(CO)_6}\)**

Carbon monoxide is a neutral ligand and the compound as a whole is neutral, so chromium is in the zero oxidation state. Six carbonyl ligands give a coordination number of 6.

\(\mathrm{EAN} = 24 - 0 + 2(6) = 24 + 12\)

\(\therefore\ \mathrm{EAN} = 36\)

Both come to 36, the atomic number of krypton, which is consistent with Sidgwick's rule and with the fact that both compounds are stable.

stem: What is effective atomic number? Calculate effective atomic number of copper (\(\text{Z} = 29\)) in \(\left\lbrack \text{Cu}\left( \text{NH}_{3} \right)_{4} \right\rbrack^{2 +}\).
solution:
**Effective atomic number (EAN)** is the total number of electrons on the central metal atom or ion of a complex AFTER it has accepted the electron pairs donated by the ligands. It is counted as

\(\mathrm{EAN} =\) (atomic number of the metal) \(-\) (oxidation state of the metal) \(+\ 2 \times\) (number of coordinate bonds formed by the ligands)

Sidgwick noticed that in many stable complexes this number comes out equal to the atomic number of the nearest noble gas.

**For \(\mathrm{[Cu(NH_3)_4]^{2\oplus}}\).**

Ammonia is a neutral ligand, so \(x + 4(0) = +2\) gives \(x = +2\), i.e. \(\mathrm{Cu^{2\oplus}}\).

Four monodentate ammine ligands donate four electron pairs, so the coordination number is 4.

\(\mathrm{EAN} = 29 - 2 + 2(4) = 29 - 2 + 8\)

\(\therefore\ \mathrm{EAN} = 35\)

Checking against the rule: krypton is 36, so 35 is not a noble gas number. This complex is one of those in which the EAN rule is not obeyed, which is why the rule is treated as a useful generalisation and not as a law.

stem: Identify complex ion in which effective atomic number of the central metal ion is \(35\). (Given \(\text{At}\). Number of \(\text{Co} = 27\), \(\text{Fe} = 26\), \(\text{Zn} = 30\)).
solution:
**(C)** \(\mathrm{[Fe(CN)_6]^{3\ominus}}\)

\(\mathrm{EAN} =\) (atomic number) \(-\) (oxidation state) \(+\ 2 \times\) (coordination number). Taking each ion in turn.

\(\mathrm{[Zn(NH_3)_4]^{2\oplus}}\) - ammonia is neutral, so zinc is \(+2\) with coordination number 4. \(\mathrm{EAN} = 30 - 2 + 8 = 36\).

\(\mathrm{[Fe(CN)_6]^{4\ominus}}\) - \(x + 6(-1) = -4\) gives \(\mathrm{Fe^{2\oplus}}\), coordination number 6. \(\mathrm{EAN} = 26 - 2 + 12 = 36\).

\(\mathrm{[Fe(CN)_6]^{3\ominus}}\) - \(x + 6(-1) = -3\) gives \(\mathrm{Fe^{3\oplus}}\), coordination number 6. \(\mathrm{EAN} = 26 - 3 + 12 = 35\).

\(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_6]^{3\oplus}}\) - ammonia is neutral, so cobalt is \(+3\) with coordination number 6. \(\mathrm{EAN} = 27 - 3 + 12 = 36\).

\(\therefore\) the ion whose central metal has \(\mathrm{EAN} = 35\) is \(\mathrm{[Fe(CN)_6]^{3\ominus}}\).

Three of the four come to 36, the krypton number; only the iron(III) ion, having given up one electron more than iron(II) from the same ligand set, falls one short.

stem: Calculate the effective atomic number (\(\text{E.A.N.}\)) of copper in \(\left\lbrack \text{Cu}\left( \text{NH}_{3} \right)_{4} \right\rbrack^{2 +}\) (\(\text{Z}\) of \(\text{Cu} = 29\)). Explain ionisation isomerism in coordination compounds with a suitable example.
solution:
**Effective atomic number of copper in \(\mathrm{[Cu(NH_3)_4]^{2\oplus}}\).**

\(\mathrm{EAN} =\) (atomic number) \(-\) (oxidation state) \(+\ 2 \times\) (coordination number).

Ammonia is neutral, so \(x + 4(0) = +2\) gives \(\mathrm{Cu^{2\oplus}}\), and four monodentate ligands give a coordination number of 4.

\(\mathrm{EAN} = 29 - 2 + 2(4) = 29 - 2 + 8\)

\(\therefore\ \mathrm{EAN} = 35\)

**Ionisation isomerism.**

**Ionisation isomers** are structural isomers in which a ligand and the counter ion have exchanged places between the coordination sphere and the ionisation sphere. They have the same molecular formula, but because each sets a different ion free on dissolving, they give different ions in solution and behave differently in a precipitation test.

**Example.**

\(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5SO_4]Br}\) and \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5Br]SO_4}\)

In the first the sulphate is bound to cobalt inside the coordination sphere and the bromide is the counter ion; in the second the two have swapped places. On dissolution:

\(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5SO_4]Br} \longrightarrow \mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5SO_4]^{\oplus}} + \mathrm{Br^{\ominus}}\)

\(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5Br]SO_4} \longrightarrow \mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5Br]^{2\oplus}} + \mathrm{SO_4^{2\ominus}}\)

So the first gives a pale yellow precipitate of \(\mathrm{AgBr}\) with silver nitrate and none with barium nitrate, while the second gives a white precipitate of \(\mathrm{BaSO_4}\) with barium nitrate and none with silver nitrate. That is how the pair is told apart.

stem: Calculate effective atomic number of \(\left\lbrack \text{Co}\left( \text{NH}_{3} \right)_{6} \right\rbrack^{3 +}\) ion.
solution:
\(\mathrm{EAN} =\) (atomic number of the metal) \(-\) (oxidation state of the metal) \(+\ 2 \times\) (number of coordinate bonds formed by the ligands).

**Oxidation state.** Ammonia is a neutral ligand, so

\(x + 6(0) = +3\), giving \(x = +3\), i.e. \(\mathrm{Co^{3\oplus}}\).

**Coordination number.** Six monodentate ammine ligands each donate one electron pair, so the coordination number is 6 and twelve electrons are gained.

**Substituting**, cobalt having atomic number 27:

\(\mathrm{EAN} = 27 - 3 + 2(6) = 27 - 3 + 12\)

\(\therefore\ \mathrm{EAN} = 36\)

The value 36 is the atomic number of krypton, the nearest noble gas, which is consistent with the EAN rule and with the marked stability of this complex ion.

stem: What is effective atomic number (EAN)? Calculate \(\text{EAN}\) of cobalt (\(\text{Z} = 27\)) in \(\left\lbrack \text{Co}\left( \text{NH}_{3} \right)_{6} \right\rbrack^{3 +}\) and of zinc (\(\text{Z} = 30\)) in \(\left\lbrack \text{Zn}\left( \text{NH}_{3} \right)_{4} \right\rbrack\text{SO}_{4}\).
solution:
**Effective atomic number (EAN)** is the total number of electrons on the central metal atom or ion of a complex AFTER it has accepted the electron pairs donated by the ligands. It is counted as

\(\mathrm{EAN} =\) (atomic number of the metal) \(-\) (oxidation state of the metal) \(+\ 2 \times\) (number of coordinate bonds formed by the ligands)

Sidgwick noticed that in many stable complexes this number comes out equal to the atomic number of the nearest noble gas.

**Cobalt in \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_6]^{3\oplus}}\).**

Ammonia is neutral, so \(x + 6(0) = +3\) gives \(\mathrm{Co^{3\oplus}}\), and six monodentate ligands give a coordination number of 6.

\(\mathrm{EAN} = 27 - 3 + 2(6) = 27 - 3 + 12\)

\(\therefore\ \mathrm{EAN} = 36\)

**Zinc in \(\mathrm{[Zn(NH_3)_4]SO_4}\).**

The sulphate ion outside the bracket carries \(2-\), so the coordination sphere is \(\mathrm{[Zn(NH_3)_4]^{2\oplus}}\), and since ammonia is neutral, \(x + 4(0) = +2\) gives \(\mathrm{Zn^{2\oplus}}\). Four monodentate ligands give a coordination number of 4.

\(\mathrm{EAN} = 30 - 2 + 2(4) = 30 - 2 + 8\)

\(\therefore\ \mathrm{EAN} = 36\)

Both come to 36, the krypton number, even though the two metals differ by three in atomic number and the two complexes differ in coordination number - the higher oxidation state of cobalt is offset by the two extra ligands it carries.

stem: The \(\text{IUPAC}\) name of \(\text{K}_{4}\left\lbrack \text{Fe}\left( \text{CN} \right)_{6} \right\rbrack\) is _____.
solution:
**(D)** potassium hexacyanoferrate

An IUPAC name is built systematically: the cation first, then the ligands in alphabetical order with their number shown by a Greek prefix, then the metal, and last its oxidation state in Roman numerals in brackets.

In \(\mathrm{K_4[Fe(CN)_6]}\) the four potassium ions carry \(+4\), so the coordination sphere is \(\mathrm{[Fe(CN)_6]^{4\ominus}}\) and

\(x + 6(-1) = -4\), giving \(x = +2\).

The sphere is negatively charged, so the metal takes the suffix 'ate' and iron becomes 'ferrate'. Six cyanide ligands give 'hexacyano'. Assembling these:

**potassium hexacyanoferrate(II)** - written hexacyanidoferrate(II) in the current recommendations.

'Potassium ferrocyanide' and 'potassium ferricyanide' are trivial names rather than systematic ones, and the second of those two names the iron(III) compound \(\mathrm{K_3[Fe(CN)_6]}\) and not this one. A numerical prefix on the potassium is never used, because how many counter ions there are follows from the charge on the sphere and is not part of the name.

\(\therefore\) the systematic name of \(\mathrm{K_4[Fe(CN)_6]}\) is potassium hexacyanoferrate, completed by the oxidation state (II).

stem: On the basis of valence bond theory explain the nature of bonding in \(\left\lbrack \text{Co}\text{F}_{6} \right\rbrack^{3 -}\) Write the \(\text{IUPAC}\) name of \(\left\lbrack \text{Co}\left( \text{NO}_{2} \right)_{3}\left( \text{NH}_{3} \right)_{3} \right\rbrack\).
solution:
**Valence bond description of \(\mathrm{[CoF_6]^{3\ominus}}\).**

**Oxidation state.** Each fluoride is \(-1\):

\(x + 6(-1) = -3\), so \(x = +3\), i.e. \(\mathrm{Co^{3\oplus}}\).

**Free metal ion.** Cobalt has atomic number 27 and the configuration \(\mathrm{[Ar]3d^7 4s^2}\), so \(\mathrm{Co^{3\oplus}}\) is \(\mathrm{3d^6}\). Writing each orbital as a box:

\(\mathrm{Co^{3\oplus}}\) (free ion)

\(\mathrm{3d} :\) \((\uparrow\downarrow)(\uparrow)(\uparrow)(\uparrow)(\uparrow)\)   \(\mathrm{4s} :\) \((\ )\)   \(\mathrm{4p} :\) \((\ )(\ )(\ )\)   \(\mathrm{4d} :\) \((\ )(\ )\)

**Nature of the ligand.** The donor atom is fluorine, a halogen, so \(\mathrm{F^{\ominus}}\) is a weak field ligand. The splitting it produces is smaller than the electron pairing energy, so the \(\mathrm{3d}\) electrons are not forced to pair and no \(\mathrm{3d}\) orbital is vacated.

**Hybridisation.** Six ligands need six vacant metal orbitals, and with the \(\mathrm{3d}\) set unavailable these must come from the outer shell - one \(\mathrm{4s}\), three \(\mathrm{4p}\) and two \(\mathrm{4d}\) - which hybridise to give six equivalent \(\mathrm{sp^3d^2}\) orbitals.

**After complex formation.**

\(\mathrm{3d} :\) \((\uparrow\downarrow)(\uparrow)(\uparrow)(\uparrow)(\uparrow)\)   \(\mathrm{4s} :\) \((\uparrow\downarrow)\)   \(\mathrm{4p} :\) \((\uparrow\downarrow)(\uparrow\downarrow)(\uparrow\downarrow)\)   \(\mathrm{4d} :\) \((\uparrow\downarrow)(\uparrow\downarrow)\)

the six pairs shown outside the \(\mathrm{3d}\) set being those donated by the six fluoride ions.

**Geometry and magnetic behaviour.** The six \(\mathrm{sp^3d^2}\) orbitals point to the corners of a regular octahedron, so the ion is **octahedral**. Because outer \(\mathrm{4d}\) orbitals are used it is an **outer orbital**, or high-spin, complex. Four unpaired electrons remain, so it is **paramagnetic**:

\(\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)} = \sqrt{4(6)} = \sqrt{24} = 4.90\ \mathrm{BM}\)

**IUPAC name of \(\mathrm{[Co(NO_2)_3(NH_3)_3]}\).**

The compound is neutral, and each nitro ligand is \(-1\) while ammonia is neutral:

\(x + 3(-1) + 3(0) = 0\), so \(x = +3\).

The ligands are named in alphabetical order, ammine before nitro, each with the prefix tri, and since the sphere is neutral the metal keeps its own name:

**triamminetrinitrocobalt(III)**

stem: Write the formula of \(\text{Tetraamminedichloroplatinum(IV) chloride}\). How is propene converted into 1-bromopropane and 2-bromopropane?
solution:
**Formula of tetraamminedichloroplatinum(IV) chloride.**

The name is read from the end backwards. The 'chloride' at the end is the counter ion, outside the coordination sphere. Inside it, 'tetraammine' is four neutral \(\mathrm{NH_3}\) and 'dichloro' is two \(\mathrm{Cl^{\ominus}}\), and the Roman numeral fixes platinum at \(+4\).

Charge on the sphere \(= +4 + 4(0) + 2(-1) = +2\)

so the sphere is \(\mathrm{[PtCl_2(NH_3)_4]^{2\oplus}}\) and two chloride ions are needed outside it to make the compound neutral.

\(\therefore\) the formula is \(\mathrm{[PtCl_2(NH_3)_4]Cl_2}\).

**Conversion of propene into 1-bromopropane and 2-bromopropane.**

Both products come from the addition of hydrogen bromide to the same alkene; which one forms is decided by whether a peroxide is present.

**2-bromopropane** - with no peroxide present the addition follows Markownikoff's rule, the hydrogen going to the doubly bonded carbon that already carries the greater number of hydrogen atoms, so the bromine lands on the middle carbon:

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH=CH_2} + \mathrm{HBr} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH_3-CHBr-CH_3}\)

**1-bromopropane** - in the presence of benzoyl peroxide the addition is anti-Markownikoff, the Kharasch peroxide effect, and the bromine adds to the terminal carbon:

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH=CH_2} + \mathrm{HBr} \xrightarrow{\text{benzoyl peroxide}} \mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-CH_2Br}\)

stem: \(\text{Fe}^{2 +}\) ions react with nitric oxide formed from reduction of nitrate and yields a brown coloured complex _____.
solution:
**(D)** \(\mathrm{[Fe(H_2O)_5NO]^{2\oplus}}\)

This is the brown ring test for a nitrate. Freshly prepared iron(II) sulphate solution is added to the nitrate, and concentrated sulphuric acid is then poured down the side of the tube. The acid reduces some of the nitrate to nitric oxide:

\(\mathrm{2NO_3^{\ominus}} + \mathrm{4H_2SO_4} + \mathrm{6Fe^{2\oplus}} \longrightarrow \mathrm{6Fe^{3\oplus}} + \mathrm{2NO} + \mathrm{4SO_4^{2\ominus}} + \mathrm{4H_2O}\)

Iron(II) sulphate in water exists as the hydrated ion \(\mathrm{[Fe(H_2O)_6]^{2\oplus}}\). The nitric oxide just formed displaces one water molecule from it and takes that place, and the resulting complex is the brown ring seen at the junction of the two layers:

\(\mathrm{[Fe(H_2O)_6]^{2\oplus}} + \mathrm{NO} \longrightarrow \mathrm{[Fe(H_2O)_5NO]^{2\oplus}} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

Since the iron enters the reaction as its aqua complex, the five ligands that remain beside the nitrosyl group are water molecules. Carbon monoxide, ammonia and methylamine are not present in the solution at all, so none of them can appear in the brown complex.

\(\therefore\) the brown complex is \(\mathrm{[Fe(H_2O)_5NO]^{2\oplus}}\).

stem: How glucose is prepared from cane sugar? Write the formula of the complex: \(\text{copper}\left( \text{II} \right)\) \(\text{hexacyanoferrate}\left( \text{II} \right)\).
solution:
**Preparation of glucose from cane sugar.**

Cane sugar is sucrose, \(\mathrm{C_{12}H_{22}O_{11}}\), a disaccharide built from one glucose unit and one fructose unit joined by a glycosidic linkage. Boiling it with dilute hydrochloric acid (or dilute sulphuric acid) in alcoholic solution hydrolyses that linkage and splits the molecule into its two monosaccharides in equal amounts:

\(\mathrm{C_{12}H_{22}O_{11}} + \mathrm{H_2O} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\text{dil. HCl}} \mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_6} + \mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_6}\)

sucrose gives D-glucose and D-fructose. The glucose is then separated by crystallisation, being the less soluble of the two in alcohol.

**Formula of copper(II) hexacyanoferrate(II).**

'Hexacyanoferrate(II)' names an anionic sphere holding six cyanide ligands, each \(-1\), round iron in the \(+2\) state:

charge on the sphere \(= +2 + 6(-1) = -4\), i.e. \(\mathrm{[Fe(CN)_6]^{4\ominus}}\)

Copper(II) supplies \(\mathrm{Cu^{2\oplus}}\), so two copper ions are needed to balance the \(4-\) charge.

\(\therefore\) the formula is \(\mathrm{Cu_2[Fe(CN)_6]}\).

stem: The correct formula for the complex compound, sodium hexacyanoferrate (\(\text{III}\)) is _____.
solution:
**\(\mathrm{Na_3[Fe(CN)_6]}\)**

'Ferrate' shows that the coordination sphere is anionic, and 'hexacyano' that six cyanide ligands are bound to the iron. The Roman numeral fixes iron at \(+3\), and each cyanide carries \(-1\):

charge on the sphere \(= +3 + 6(-1) = -3\), i.e. \(\mathrm{[Fe(CN)_6]^{3\ominus}}\)

Three sodium ions are needed outside the bracket to make the compound electrically neutral.

\(\therefore\) the formula of sodium hexacyanoferrate(III) is \(\mathrm{Na_3[Fe(CN)_6]}\).

Testing the rest: \(\mathrm{Na[Fe(CN)_6]}\) and \(\mathrm{Na_2[Fe(CN)_6]}\) would leave the sphere at \(1-\) and \(2-\), which would need iron in the \(+5\) and \(+4\) states, and \(\mathrm{Na_4[Fe(CN)_6]}\) is the iron(II) compound, sodium hexacyanoferrate(II).

stem: The correct formula of a complex having \(\text{IUPAC}\) name Tetraamminedibromoplatinum (\(\text{IV}\)) bromide is _____.
solution:
**(C)** \(\mathrm{[PtBr_2(NH_3)_4]Br_2}\)

Read the name from the end backwards. The 'bromide' at the end is the counter ion outside the sphere; 'tetraammine' is four neutral \(\mathrm{NH_3}\) and 'dibromo' is two \(\mathrm{Br^{\ominus}}\) inside it, and (IV) fixes platinum at \(+4\).

Charge on the coordination sphere \(= +4 + 4(0) + 2(-1) = +2\)

so the sphere is \(\mathrm{[PtBr_2(NH_3)_4]^{2\oplus}}\) and two bromide ions are needed outside it.

\(\therefore\) the formula is \(\mathrm{[PtBr_2(NH_3)_4]Br_2}\).

Testing the rest: the two formulae written with a single bromide inside the sphere contradict the prefix 'di', and \(\mathrm{[PtBr_2(NH_3)_4]Br}\) leaves a \(2+\) sphere balanced by only one \(1-\) ion, so it is not electrically neutral. Collecting the whole formula, \(\mathrm{PtBr_4(NH_3)_4}\), and putting all four bromides at \(-1\) returns platinum to \(+4\), as the name states.

stem: The correct structure of complex having \(\text{IUPAC}\) name sodium hexanitrocobaltate (\(\text{III}\)) is _____.
solution:
**(C)** \(\mathrm{Na_3[Co(NO_2)_6]}\)

'Cobaltate' shows that the coordination sphere is anionic, and 'hexanitro' that six nitro ligands \(\mathrm{NO_2^{\ominus}}\), each \(-1\), are bound to the cobalt, which the Roman numeral fixes at \(+3\).

Charge on the sphere \(= +3 + 6(-1) = -3\), i.e. \(\mathrm{[Co(NO_2)_6]^{3\ominus}}\)

Three sodium ions balance it.

\(\therefore\) the formula is \(\mathrm{Na_3[Co(NO_2)_6]}\).

Testing the rest: the two formulae written with only five nitro ligands contradict the prefix 'hexa', and \(\mathrm{Na_4[Co(NO_2)_6]}\) would make the sphere \(4-\), which needs cobalt in the \(+2\) state and not the \(+3\) the name gives.

stem: Explain the geometry of \(\left\lbrack \text{Co}\left( \text{NH}_{3} \right)_{6} \right\rbrack^{3 +}\) on the basis of hybridisation. (\(\text{Z}\) of \(\text{Co} = 27\)).
solution:
**Oxidation state.** Ammonia is a neutral ligand, so

\(x + 6(0) = +3\), giving \(x = +3\), i.e. \(\mathrm{Co^{3\oplus}}\).

**Free metal ion.** Cobalt has atomic number 27 and the configuration \(\mathrm{[Ar]3d^7 4s^2}\), so \(\mathrm{Co^{3\oplus}}\) is \(\mathrm{3d^6}\). Writing each orbital as a box:

\(\mathrm{Co^{3\oplus}}\) (free ion)

\(\mathrm{3d} :\) \((\uparrow\downarrow)(\uparrow)(\uparrow)(\uparrow)(\uparrow)\)   \(\mathrm{4s} :\) \((\ )\)   \(\mathrm{4p} :\) \((\ )(\ )(\ )\)

**Nature of the ligand.** The donor atom of ammonia is nitrogen, so \(\mathrm{NH_3}\) is a strong field ligand. The splitting it produces is larger than the electron pairing energy, so the four unpaired \(\mathrm{3d}\) electrons are forced to pair and two of the five \(\mathrm{3d}\) orbitals are left vacant:

\(\mathrm{3d} :\) \((\uparrow\downarrow)(\uparrow\downarrow)(\uparrow\downarrow)(\ )(\ )\)

**Hybridisation.** Six ammine ligands need six vacant orbitals. The two vacated \(\mathrm{3d}\) orbitals, together with the \(\mathrm{4s}\) and the three \(\mathrm{4p}\) orbitals, hybridise to give six equivalent \(\mathrm{d^2sp^3}\) orbitals.

**After complex formation.**

\(\mathrm{3d} :\) \((\uparrow\downarrow)(\uparrow\downarrow)(\uparrow\downarrow)(\uparrow\downarrow)(\uparrow\downarrow)\)   \(\mathrm{4s} :\) \((\uparrow\downarrow)\)   \(\mathrm{4p} :\) \((\uparrow\downarrow)(\uparrow\downarrow)(\uparrow\downarrow)\)

the last six pairs being the electron pairs donated by the six ammonia molecules.

**Geometry.** The six \(\mathrm{d^2sp^3}\) hybrid orbitals point to the corners of a regular octahedron, so \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_6]^{3\oplus}}\) is **octahedral**. Because inner \(\mathrm{3d}\) orbitals are used it is an inner orbital, or low-spin, complex, and since every electron is paired it is diamagnetic, with \(\mu = 0\).

stem: Explain formation of \(\left\lbrack \text{CoF}_{6} \right\rbrack^{3 -}\) complex with respect to _______.
solution:
**Valence bond treatment of \(\mathrm{[CoF_6]^{3\ominus}}\).**

**Oxidation state.** Each fluoride is \(-1\), so \(x + 6(-1) = -3\) gives \(x = +3\), i.e. \(\mathrm{Co^{3\oplus}}\).

**Free metal ion.** Cobalt has atomic number 27, \(\mathrm{[Ar]3d^7 4s^2}\), so \(\mathrm{Co^{3\oplus}}\) is \(\mathrm{3d^6}\):

\(\mathrm{3d} :\) \((\uparrow\downarrow)(\uparrow)(\uparrow)(\uparrow)(\uparrow)\)   \(\mathrm{4s} :\) \((\ )\)   \(\mathrm{4p} :\) \((\ )(\ )(\ )\)   \(\mathrm{4d} :\) \((\ )(\ )\)

**Hybridisation.** The donor atom is fluorine, a halogen, so \(\mathrm{F^{\ominus}}\) is a weak field ligand: the splitting it produces is smaller than the electron pairing energy, the \(\mathrm{3d}\) electrons are not forced to pair, and no \(\mathrm{3d}\) orbital is vacated. The six vacant orbitals the six ligands need must therefore be taken from the outer shell - one \(\mathrm{4s}\), three \(\mathrm{4p}\) and two \(\mathrm{4d}\) - giving **\(\mathrm{sp^3d^2}\)** hybridisation.

After the six fluoride ions have donated their electron pairs:

\(\mathrm{3d} :\) \((\uparrow\downarrow)(\uparrow)(\uparrow)(\uparrow)(\uparrow)\)   \(\mathrm{4s} :\) \((\uparrow\downarrow)\)   \(\mathrm{4p} :\) \((\uparrow\downarrow)(\uparrow\downarrow)(\uparrow\downarrow)\)   \(\mathrm{4d} :\) \((\uparrow\downarrow)(\uparrow\downarrow)\)

**Magnetic property.** Four unpaired electrons remain in the \(\mathrm{3d}\) set, so the complex is **paramagnetic**:

\(\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)} = \sqrt{4(6)} = \sqrt{24}\)

\(\therefore\ \mu = 4.90\ \mathrm{BM}\)

**Inner or outer orbital complex.** The hybridisation uses the OUTER \(\mathrm{4d}\) orbitals rather than the inner \(\mathrm{3d}\) ones, so \(\mathrm{[CoF_6]^{3\ominus}}\) is an **outer orbital**, or high-spin, complex.

**Geometry.** Six \(\mathrm{sp^3d^2}\) hybrid orbitals point to the corners of a regular octahedron, so the complex is **octahedral**.

Set beside it, \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_6]^{3\oplus}}\) has the same \(\mathrm{Co^{3\oplus}}\) ion meeting the strong field ligand ammonia: there the \(\mathrm{3d}\) electrons pair, two inner \(\mathrm{3d}\) orbitals are vacated, the hybridisation is \(\mathrm{d^2sp^3}\), and the octahedral complex is inner orbital and diamagnetic. The whole difference is made by the field strength of the ligand.

stem: Mention the number of unpaired electrons and geometry of following complexes: (i) \(\left\lbrack \text{Ni}\left( \text{Cl} \right)_{4} \right\rbrack^{2 -}\) (ii) \(\left\lbrack \text{Ni}\left( \text{CN} \right)_{4} \right\rbrack^{2 -}\).
solution:
Nickel has atomic number 28 and the configuration \(\mathrm{[Ar]3d^8 4s^2}\), and in both complexes the metal ion turns out to be the same, so the whole difference is made by the ligand.

**(i) \(\mathrm{[NiCl_4]^{2\ominus}}\)**

Oxidation state: \(x + 4(-1) = -2\), so \(x = +2\), i.e. \(\mathrm{Ni^{2\oplus}}\), a \(\mathrm{3d^8}\) ion:

\(\mathrm{3d} :\) \((\uparrow\downarrow)(\uparrow\downarrow)(\uparrow\downarrow)(\uparrow)(\uparrow)\)

Chloride is a weak field ligand, so the \(\mathrm{3d}\) electrons are left undisturbed and no \(\mathrm{3d}\) orbital is vacated. The four vacant orbitals the four ligands need must come from the outer shell - one \(\mathrm{4s}\) and three \(\mathrm{4p}\) - giving \(\mathrm{sp^3}\) hybridisation.

**Unpaired electrons: 2. Geometry: tetrahedral.** The ion is paramagnetic, with \(\mu = \sqrt{2(4)} = \sqrt{8} = 2.83\ \mathrm{BM}\).

**(ii) \(\mathrm{[Ni(CN)_4]^{2\ominus}}\)**

Oxidation state: \(x + 4(-1) = -2\), so again \(\mathrm{Ni^{2\oplus}}\), \(\mathrm{3d^8}\).

Cyanide is a strong field ligand, so the two unpaired \(\mathrm{3d}\) electrons are forced to pair, and this vacates one \(\mathrm{3d}\) orbital:

\(\mathrm{3d} :\) \((\uparrow\downarrow)(\uparrow\downarrow)(\uparrow\downarrow)(\uparrow\downarrow)(\ )\)

That vacant \(\mathrm{3d}\) orbital, with the \(\mathrm{4s}\) and two of the \(\mathrm{4p}\) orbitals, gives four \(\mathrm{dsp^2}\) hybrid orbitals lying in one plane at \(90^\circ\) to one another.

**Unpaired electrons: 0. Geometry: square planar.** The ion is diamagnetic, with \(\mu = 0\).

Both complexes have the same central ion and the same coordination number of four, so the difference in both answers traces back to one thing only, the field strength of the ligand.

stem: Which of the following complexes will give a white precipitate on treatment with a solution of barium nitrate?
solution:
[Board paper defect: as printed, \(\mathrm{[Cr(NH_3)_4SO_4]Cl}\) and \(\mathrm{[Cr(NH_3)_4Cl]SO_4}\) leave chromium with a coordination number of five, whereas chromium(III) is six-coordinate everywhere else in the chapter; the pair the paper almost certainly carried is \(\mathrm{[Cr(NH_3)_5SO_4]Cl}\) and \(\mathrm{[Cr(NH_3)_5Cl]SO_4}\). Preserved as printed. The reasoning and the answer are unchanged either way, since only one of the four sets sulphate free outside the coordination sphere.]

**(C)** \(\mathrm{[Cr(NH_3)_4Cl]SO_4}\)

Barium nitrate gives a white precipitate of barium sulphate:

\(\mathrm{Ba^{2\oplus}} + \mathrm{SO_4^{2\ominus}} \longrightarrow \mathrm{BaSO_4} \downarrow\)

so the test succeeds only if the complex sets free sulphate ions in solution. Only what lies OUTSIDE the square bracket, in the ionisation sphere, is set free; a sulphate bound to the metal inside the coordination sphere is non-ionisable and gives no precipitate at all.

Examining each complex on that basis:

\(\mathrm{[Cr(NH_3)_4SO_4]Cl}\) - the sulphate is a ligand inside the sphere and the ionisable ion is chloride, so it precipitates with silver nitrate and not with barium nitrate.

\(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_4Cl_2]NO_2}\) - carries no sulphate at all.

\(\mathrm{[Cr(NH_3)_4Cl]SO_4}\) - the sulphate is the counter ion and is free in solution. Checking the charge, \(x + 4(0) + (-1) = +2\) gives \(\mathrm{Cr^{3\oplus}}\), so the sphere really is \(2+\) and is balanced by one \(\mathrm{SO_4^{2\ominus}}\).

\(\mathrm{[CrCl_2(H_2O)_4]Cl}\) - carries no sulphate at all.

\(\therefore\) only \(\mathrm{[Cr(NH_3)_4Cl]SO_4}\) gives a white precipitate with barium nitrate.

\(\mathrm{[Cr(NH_3)_4SO_4]Cl}\) and \(\mathrm{[Cr(NH_3)_4Cl]SO_4}\) have the same molecular formula and differ only in which of the two ions sits inside the sphere, so they are ionisation isomers, and this is exactly the test that tells such a pair apart.

stem: What is the geometry of chromate ion?
solution:
**(A)** Tetrahedral

The chromate ion is \(\mathrm{CrO_4^{2\ominus}}\). Taking the oxidation state of chromium, each oxygen being \(-2\):

\(x + 4(-2) = -2\), so \(x = +6\), i.e. \(\mathrm{Cr^{6\oplus}}\)

Chromium is \(\mathrm{[Ar]3d^5 4s^1}\), so \(\mathrm{Cr^{6\oplus}}\) has given up every valence electron and is a \(\mathrm{3d^0}\) ion. Four oxygen atoms are bound to it, so four orbitals are needed, and they are taken as one \(\mathrm{4s}\) and three \(\mathrm{4p}\).

\(\mathrm{sp^3}\) hybridisation directs those four orbitals to the corners of a regular tetrahedron, with a bond angle of \(109^\circ 28'\).

\(\therefore\) the chromate ion is tetrahedral.

An octahedral or a linear shape would call for a coordination number of six or two, and a trigonal planar shape for a coordination number of three, whereas the chromium here is surrounded by exactly four oxygen atoms.

stem: Calculate the effective atomic number (e.a.n.) of copper in \(\left\lbrack \text{Cu}\left( \text{NH}_{3} \right)_{4} \right\rbrack^{2 +}.\ \lbrack Z\ of\ Cu\ = 29\rbrack\) Explain linkage isomerism in coordination compounds with a suitable example.
solution:
**Effective atomic number of copper in \(\mathrm{[Cu(NH_3)_4]^{2\oplus}}\).**

\(\mathrm{EAN} =\) (atomic number) \(-\) (oxidation state) \(+\ 2 \times\) (coordination number).

Ammonia is neutral, so \(x + 4(0) = +2\) gives \(\mathrm{Cu^{2\oplus}}\), and four monodentate ligands give a coordination number of 4.

\(\mathrm{EAN} = 29 - 2 + 2(4) = 29 - 2 + 8\)

\(\therefore\ \mathrm{EAN} = 35\)

**Linkage isomerism.**

**Linkage isomers** are structural isomers that arise when an ambidentate ligand - one carrying more than one kind of donor atom - binds to the metal through a different donor atom in each isomer. The molecular formula is the same in both; only the atom through which the ligand is attached differs, and with it the colour and other properties of the complex.

**Example.** The nitrite ion \(\mathrm{NO_2^{\ominus}}\) can bind either through its nitrogen atom or through one of its oxygen atoms:

\(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5(NO_2)]^{2\oplus}}\) - bound through nitrogen, the nitro isomer, which is yellow

\(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5(ONO)]^{2\oplus}}\) - bound through oxygen, the nitrito isomer, which is red

The thiocyanate ion \(\mathrm{SCN^{\ominus}}\) behaves in the same way, binding either through sulphur, as thiocyanato, or through nitrogen, as isothiocyanato.

stem: Define: Distereoisomers. Give cis and trans isomers of \(\left\lbrack \text{Co}\left( \text{NH}_{3} \right)_{4}\text{Cl}_{2} \right\rbrack^{+}\).
solution:
**Diastereoisomers** are stereoisomers that are NOT mirror images of each other. They share the same molecular formula and the same connectivity but differ in the arrangement of the ligands in space, and because they are not related as object and mirror image they differ in physical properties such as colour, melting point and solubility. The geometric isomers of a coordination compound, the cis and the trans forms, are diastereoisomers of each other.

**Isomers of \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_4Cl_2]^{\oplus}}\).**

Ammonia is neutral and each chloride is \(-1\):

\(x + 4(0) + 2(-1) = +1\), so \(x = +3\), i.e. \(\mathrm{Co^{3\oplus}}\)

with a coordination number of six - an octahedral complex of the \(\mathrm{MA_4B_2}\) type, which the chapter says exists as a cis and a trans form.

Draw cobalt at the centre of an octahedron with the six ligands at its vertices, four in the square plane and one directly above and one directly below.

*cis isomer* - the two chloride ligands take ADJACENT vertices, so that the angle \(\mathrm{Cl-Co-Cl}\) is \(90^\circ\), and the four ammine ligands fill the remaining four positions. This form is violet.

*trans isomer* - the two chloride ligands take OPPOSITE vertices, so that \(\mathrm{Cl-Co-Cl}\) is \(180^\circ\), and the four ammine ligands lie in the square plane between them. This form is green.

Neither form is chiral, since each has a plane of symmetry, so the two are related as diastereoisomers and not as enantiomers - which is what the definition above requires.

stem: When excess of \(\text{AgNO}_{3}\) is added to a complex, one mole of \(\text{AgCl}\) is precipitated. The formula of complex is _____.
solution:
**(A)** \(\mathrm{[CoCl_2(NH_3)_4]Cl}\)

Only the chloride ions in the ionisation sphere - those written OUTSIDE the square bracket - are free in solution and available to be precipitated:

\(\mathrm{Ag^{\oplus}} + \mathrm{Cl^{\ominus}} \longrightarrow \mathrm{AgCl} \downarrow\)

Chloride bound to the metal inside the coordination sphere is non-ionisable and gives no precipitate. Since the silver nitrate is in excess, the number of moles of \(\mathrm{AgCl}\) formed per mole of complex is simply the number of chlorides written outside the bracket.

Counting them:

\(\mathrm{[CoCl_2(NH_3)_4]Cl}\) - one outside, so 1 mole of \(\mathrm{AgCl}\)

\(\mathrm{[CoCl(NH_3)_5]Cl_2}\) - two outside, so 2 moles

\(\mathrm{[CoCl_3(NH_3)_3]}\) - none outside, so no precipitate at all

\(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_6]Cl_3}\) - three outside, so 3 moles

\(\therefore\) the complex is \(\mathrm{[CoCl_2(NH_3)_4]Cl}\).

It is consistent in the other respects too: \(x + 2(-1) + 4(0) = +1\) gives cobalt \(+3\), with a coordination number of six.

stem: Explain ionization isomers with suitable example in complexes.
solution:
**Ionisation isomers** are structural isomers in which a ligand and the counter ion have exchanged places between the coordination sphere and the ionisation sphere. They have the same molecular formula, but because each sets a different ion free on dissolving, they give different ions in solution and so behave differently towards a precipitating reagent.

**Example.**

\(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5SO_4]Br}\) and \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5Br]SO_4}\)

In the first the sulphate is bound to cobalt inside the coordination sphere and the bromide is the counter ion; in the second the two have swapped places. Both have the molecular formula \(\mathrm{CoH_{15}N_5SO_4Br}\), yet on dissolution they ionise differently:

\(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5SO_4]Br} \longrightarrow \mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5SO_4]^{\oplus}} + \mathrm{Br^{\ominus}}\)

\(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5Br]SO_4} \longrightarrow \mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5Br]^{2\oplus}} + \mathrm{SO_4^{2\ominus}}\)

So the first gives a pale yellow precipitate of \(\mathrm{AgBr}\) with silver nitrate and nothing with barium nitrate, while the second gives a white precipitate of \(\mathrm{BaSO_4}\) with barium nitrate and nothing with silver nitrate. Testing with the two reagents therefore tells the pair apart.

stem: Explain the term: a. Optical activity b. Ligand c. Interstitial compounds
solution:
**a. Optical activity.**

A substance is optically active when it can rotate the plane of plane-polarised light passed through it. A coordination compound shows optical activity when the complex and its mirror image are non-superimposable, that is, when the complex possesses neither a plane nor a centre of symmetry. Such a complex is said to be chiral, and the two non-superimposable mirror images are called enantiomers, or the d and l forms; they rotate the plane by equal amounts in opposite directions. \(\mathrm{cis}\)-\(\mathrm{[Co(en)_2Cl_2]^{\oplus}}\) is an example, while the trans form of the same complex has a plane of symmetry and is optically inactive.

**b. Ligand.**

A ligand is the ion or molecule bound to the central metal atom or ion of a coordination compound through a coordinate bond. It is the ligand that supplies the shared electron pair, so a ligand is an electron pair donor, that is, a Lewis base. \(\mathrm{Cl^{\ominus}}\), \(\mathrm{CN^{\ominus}}\), \(\mathrm{NH_3}\) and \(\mathrm{H_2O}\) bind through a single donor atom and are monodentate; ethylenediamine and the oxalate ion bind through two and are bidentate; \(\mathrm{EDTA^{4\ominus}}\) binds through six and is hexadentate.

**c. Interstitial compounds.**

These are the compounds formed when small atoms such as hydrogen, carbon, nitrogen or boron are trapped in the interstitial voids of the crystal lattice of a transition metal. They are usually non-stoichiometric, so a definite formula cannot be written for them; they keep the metallic conductivity of the parent metal, and they are harder, less malleable and higher melting than it, because the trapped atoms make the metal lattice more rigid. \(\mathrm{TiC}\), \(\mathrm{Mn_4N}\) and \(\mathrm{Fe_3H}\) are examples.

stem: The ligand diethylenetriamine is _____.
solution:
**(C)** tridentate

The denticity of a ligand is the number of donor atoms by which one molecule or ion of it binds to the same central metal ion.

Diethylenetriamine, usually written 'dien', is

\(\mathrm{H_2N-CH_2-CH_2-NH-CH_2-CH_2-NH_2}\)

and its name says the same thing: two ethylene bridges joining three amine nitrogen atoms.

Each of those three nitrogen atoms carries a lone pair, and all three can be donated to the same metal ion at once - the two terminal \(\mathrm{-NH_2}\) groups and the central \(\mathrm{-NH-}\) group.

\(\therefore\) diethylenetriamine has three donor atoms and is a tridentate ligand, contributing 3 to the coordination number of the metal.

Counting the same way, ethylenediamine with two nitrogen atoms is bidentate, and \(\mathrm{EDTA^{4\ominus}}\), with two nitrogen and four carboxylate oxygen donor atoms, is hexadentate.

stem: Write the name of the platinum complex used in the treatment of cancer.
solution:
**Cisplatin** - the cis isomer of diamminedichloroplatinum(II), \(\mathrm{cis}\)-\(\mathrm{[Pt(NH_3)_2Cl_2]}\).

It is a neutral square planar complex with platinum in the \(+2\) oxidation state, carrying two ammine and two chloro ligands. Only the cis isomer, in which the two chloride ligands occupy adjacent corners of the square, is active; the trans isomer, with the two chlorides opposite each other, has no anti-cancer action at all. Cisplatin works by binding to the DNA of the tumour cell and so preventing its replication.

stem: Write postulates of Werner theory of co-ordination complexes. Write the name of a hexadentate ligand.
solution:
**Postulates of Werner's theory of coordination compounds.**

1. The central metal atom or ion of a coordination compound shows two kinds of valency: a primary valency and a secondary valency.

2. The **primary valency** is ionisable and is satisfied by negative ions. It corresponds to the oxidation state of the metal, and is shown by a dotted line in Werner's representation.

3. The **secondary valency** is non-ionisable and is satisfied by ligands, which may be negative ions or neutral molecules. It corresponds to the coordination number of the metal, and is shown by a full line.

4. Every metal has a fixed number of secondary valencies, so the coordination number of a given metal ion is fixed.

5. The secondary valencies are directed towards fixed positions in space, and it is this that gives a complex its definite geometry - a coordination number of six gives an octahedral arrangement, and a coordination number of four a tetrahedral or a square planar one.

**A hexadentate ligand.**

The ethylenediaminetetraacetate ion, \(\mathrm{EDTA^{4\ominus}}\). It holds the metal through six donor atoms - the two nitrogen atoms of its ethylenediamine backbone and one oxygen atom from each of its four carboxylate arms - so a single molecule of it can fill all six positions of an octahedral complex.

stem: Write the number of donor atoms present in \(\text{EDTA}\), during formation of complex.
solution:
**Six.**

EDTA is the ethylenediaminetetraacetate ion, \(\mathrm{EDTA^{4\ominus}}\). Its skeleton is an ethylenediamine unit, each of whose two nitrogen atoms carries two acetate arms. Counting the atoms that can donate an electron pair:

two nitrogen atoms, each with a lone pair on it, one at each end of the \(\mathrm{-CH_2-CH_2-}\) bridge

four carboxylate oxygen atoms, one from each of the four \(\mathrm{-CH_2COO^{\ominus}}\) groups

Every one of these six atoms donates a lone pair to the metal ion during complex formation.

\(\therefore\) EDTA uses \(2 + 4 = 6\) donor atoms, which is why it is called a hexadentate ligand and contributes 6 to the coordination number of the metal - enough for one EDTA molecule to fill all six positions of an octahedral complex such as \(\mathrm{[Ca(EDTA)]^{2\ominus}}\).

stem: Explain cationic, anionic and neutral sphere complexes with example.
solution:
Complexes are classified in this way by the charge carried by the coordination sphere, the part written inside the square bracket.

**Cationic sphere complex** - the coordination sphere carries a net positive charge, so the counter ion outside the bracket is an anion.
**Example:** \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_6]Cl_3}\). Ammonia is neutral, so \(x + 6(0) = +3\) makes the sphere \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_6]^{3\oplus}}\), balanced by three chloride ions. \(\mathrm{[Cu(NH_3)_4]^{2\oplus}}\) is another.

**Anionic sphere complex** - the coordination sphere carries a net negative charge, so the counter ion is a cation, and in the name the metal takes the suffix 'ate'.
**Example:** \(\mathrm{K_4[Fe(CN)_6]}\). Each cyanide is \(-1\), so \(+2 + 6(-1) = -4\) makes the sphere \(\mathrm{[Fe(CN)_6]^{4\ominus}}\), balanced by four potassium ions. \(\mathrm{[Ni(CN)_4]^{2\ominus}}\) is another.

**Neutral sphere complex** - the charge on the metal ion and the charges on the ligands cancel exactly, so the sphere carries no charge and there is no counter ion at all.
**Example:** \(\mathrm{[Ni(CO)_4]}\), in which nickel is in the zero oxidation state and all four carbonyl ligands are neutral. \(\mathrm{[Pt(NH_3)_2Cl_2]}\) is another: platinum is \(+2\), the two chloride ligands \(-1\) each and the two ammine ligands neutral, so \(+2 + 2(-1) + 2(0) = 0\).

stem: Calculate spin only magnetic moment of divalent cation of transition metal with atomic number 25. Salts of \(\text{Ti}^{4 +}\) are colorless. Give a reazson.
solution:
**Spin only magnetic moment of the divalent cation.**

The element of atomic number 25 is manganese, \(\mathrm{[Ar]3d^5 4s^2}\). A transition metal loses its \(\mathrm{4s}\) electrons first, so the divalent cation is

\(\mathrm{Mn^{2\oplus}} = \mathrm{[Ar]3d^5}\)

Following Hund's rule the five \(\mathrm{3d}\) electrons occupy the five d orbitals singly before any of them pairs:

\(\mathrm{3d} :\) \((\uparrow)(\uparrow)(\uparrow)(\uparrow)(\uparrow)\)

so the number of unpaired electrons is \(n = 5\), and the spin only magnetic moment is

\(\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)} = \sqrt{5(5+2)} = \sqrt{35}\)

\(\therefore\ \mu = 5.92\ \mathrm{BM}\)

Squaring back, \(5.92^2 \approx 35\), which is \(n(n+2)\) for \(n = 5\), so the value is consistent. It is also the largest spin only moment any first-row transition metal ion can show, since five is the greatest number of unpaired d electrons available.

**Why salts of \(\mathrm{Ti^{4\oplus}}\) are colourless.**

Titanium has atomic number 22 and the configuration \(\mathrm{[Ar]3d^2 4s^2}\), so on losing four electrons

\(\mathrm{Ti^{4\oplus}} = \mathrm{[Ar]3d^0}\)

Colour in a transition metal salt arises from a d-d transition: an electron in a lower d orbital absorbs a quantum of visible light and is promoted to a higher one, and the salt then shows the colour complementary to the light absorbed. \(\mathrm{Ti^{4\oplus}}\) has no d electron at all, so no such promotion is possible, no visible light is absorbed, and its salts are colourless.
